title: Names for the Hungarians
fact_summary: The written sources on this map call the Hungarians by several names: Ungri, Hungarii, Ungarii, in Bavaria and Saxony also “Avars”, and in Greek “Turks”. They call themselves Magyars.

claims.text: The Annals of St-Bertin, under 862, name raiders “qui Ungri vocantur” (who are called Ungri).
claims.certainty_reason: This records what the source says. The passage was read in the open copy linked under Sources.

claims.text: Regino of Prüm, under 889, writes of the “gens Hungarium”, the people of the Hungarians.
claims.certainty_reason: This records what the source says. The passage was read in the open copy linked under Sources.

claims.text: The Annals of St Vincent at Metz, under 955, call them “Ungarii”.
claims.certainty_reason: This records what the source says. The passage was read in the open copy linked under Sources.

claims.text: The Byzantine De Administrando Imperio calls them “Turks” (türkök in Tóth's Hungarian).

sources.locator: summary of DAI ch. 38 (exact page not fixed in the copy read)

claims.certainty_reason: Read only as Tóth summarises and quotes the chapter in Hungarian.

claims.text: Modern studies give both names side by side, as in “the Hungarians (Magyars)” and “Hungarians or Magyars”.
claims.certainty_reason: This records what the study reports, read in the open copy linked under Sources.

claims.text: The Ungri of the 862 annal were the Hungarians.

held_by.who: The editors of the Mapping Medieval Peoples database, who index the name under the Hungarians

claims.certainty_reason: A standard identification, but the annal itself says only that these enemies were new.

claims.text: The Bavarian continuation of the Annals of Fulda calls them “Avari, qui dicuntur Ungari”, Avars who are called Hungarians, from 894 to 900.
claims.certainty_reason: This records what the source says. The passage was read in Latin in the scanned edition linked under Sources; the English is Claude's own rendering.

claims.text: Widukind of Corvey, in the 960s, writes “Avares, quos modo Ungarios vocamus”, the Avars whom we now call Hungarians, and uses both names.
claims.certainty_reason: This records what the source says. The passage was read in Latin in the scanned edition linked under Sources; the English is Claude's own rendering.

claims.text: The Gesta Hungarorum, about 1200, promises to explain why the people “are called Hungarians in the speech of foreigners but Magyars [Mogerii] in their own”. Its answer for the first name is the castle of Ung; for the second, Magog, first king of Scythia.
claims.certainty_reason: This records what the source says, read in Martyn Rady's English translation in the open copy linked under Sources. The Latin has not been compared.

open_questions.text: Where do the Latin names Ungri and Hungarii come from, and why did a Greek writer call the Hungarians Turks?

When is the name Magyar first written down? The oldest text read so far that gives it is the Gesta Hungarorum of about 1200 (as Moger, Mogerii). Earlier witnesses, such as Arabic geographers, have not been read.

review.note: Checked by Claude against open copies of every source. Marc spot-checks a sample.
